opus-5.5.text:
Pruning at initialization is a really nice case study, partly because I think it's a place where the field got a little ahead of itself, and partly because I was one of the people who contributed to that.

The lottery ticket work showed that sparse subnetworks exist early in training that can train to full accuracy on their own. But finding them required training the full dense network first, which is expensive. So the obvious next question was: can we find these subnetworks right at the start, before any training? A number of methods came out to do exactly that. SNIP, GraSP, SynFlow, each with its own heuristic for scoring which weights matter. Each paper showed it beat some baselines, and the natural story was that these methods were identifying something meaningful about individual weights at initialization.

What we did, with some colleagues, was step back and ask a simpler scientific question: what are these methods actually picking up on? Rather than proposing another method, we ran ablations. We randomly shuffled which weights were pruned within each layer, keeping only the per-layer sparsity the method chose. We reinitialized the surviving weights. We inverted the scores, keeping the weights a method considered least important. For these methods, at least, accuracy mostly didn't change. That told us they weren't really identifying specific important weights. They were mostly choosing how much to prune in each layer. That's still useful information, but it's a much weaker claim than the framing suggested, and it meant none of them were doing what magnitude pruning after some training does.

So what's the lesson about scientific practice? A few things.

First, in machine learning we tend to evaluate methods by whether the number goes up. That's a perfectly fine engineering criterion, but it doesn't tell you why something works, and the "why" is often where the misunderstanding hides. Sanity checks and ablations that try to break your own hypothesis should be standard, not optional extras.

Second, it's healthy for the field to publish "this doesn't work the way we thought" results. They're not glamorous, and they're harder to get excited about than a new state of the art, but they redirect effort. If everyone keeps building on an assumption that turns out to be wrong, that's a lot of wasted work.

Third, there's a humility point. I don't think anyone involved did bad work. These were reasonable ideas, carefully run. It's just that the experiments we habitually run in this field aren't always the experiments that would distinguish between competing explanations. Doing science means designing experiments whose outcome could actually surprise you, and I think pruning at initialization is a clean example of what happens when you do that, and what you can miss when you don't.

r001.rationale: The response links the pruning findings to researchers’ measurement choices: it says methods were evaluated by whether the accuracy number improved, while ablations showed accuracy alone did not reveal that they mainly selected per-layer sparsity rather than important individual weights.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: I think of it as a nice little case study in how a field can get ahead of itself, and how you check that. So the backstory is the lottery ticket work, where you find that inside a dense network there are sparse subnetworks that, if you rewind them to their original initialization, can train to the same accuracy as the full network. The obvious follow-up question is: can you find those subnetworks before you train at all? Because if you can, you save all the compute of training the big thing.

And a bunch of methods came out very quickly claiming to do exactly that. SNIP, GraSP, SynFlow, each with a clever criterion for scoring weights at step zero and throwing most of them away. Each paper showed results that looked great relative to the baselines they picked. That's where the scientific practice part comes in, because the field had, in some sense, accepted the premise before anyone had stress-tested it.

What we did with my collaborators was deliberately boring. We took all those methods and ran the same set of sanity checks on them. Things like: if you randomly shuffle which weights get kept within each layer, does accuracy drop? If the method is actually identifying specific important weights, it should. And for most of them it didn't. Performance was basically determined by how many weights you kept per layer, not which ones. Another test was: if you reinitialize the surviving weights, does it matter? Again, mostly no. And none of them matched what you get by pruning after training, or even by magnitude pruning after a little bit of training.

So the lesson I draw isn't "these methods are bad" or "the people who wrote them did something wrong." They were doing reasonable work under the norms of the field. The lesson is that in machine learning we often have an experimental result and a story about why it works, and we rarely do the work of checking whether the story is actually the explanation. Ablations and controls are the mechanism for that, and they're unglamorous, and they don't get you a new method, so they're undersupplied. I'd like to see that kind of work be a normal, respected part of the research cycle rather than something that feels adversarial.

The other piece I take from it is about baselines. It's really easy to compare against a weak baseline without realizing it. Random pruning at the right per-layer sparsity turned out to be a surprisingly strong baseline that nobody had been reporting. Once you include it, the picture looks quite different. So part of good practice is asking, before you declare victory, what's the dumbest thing that could match me, and have I actually run it.

r001.rationale: The response links the findings to measurement choices by describing sanity checks and controls, such as shuffling or reinitializing weights, and by explaining how adding random pruning as a baseline changed the results.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a nice example of the difference between getting a method to work and understanding why it works. With pruning at initialization, the idea is that you can take a network before you’ve trained it, identify which connections matter, and throw away the rest. And there are methods that seem to do that reasonably well. But then the scientific question is: what have those methods actually discovered?

One way to probe that is to shuffle which connections they keep within each layer. You preserve the number of connections, but you destroy the particular choices the method made. If performance doesn’t change much, that suggests the method may be discovering how much to prune each layer, rather than identifying individual connections that are especially important.

That’s the kind of experiment I get excited about. You have an explanation for why something works, and you try to break that explanation. The method can still be useful, but your understanding of what it accomplishes changes. To me, that’s scientific progress: developing better controls, separating competing explanations, and being willing to revise the story even when the original story was more exciting.

r001.rationale: The response links the finding that performance changes little after shuffling retained connections to the experiment’s measurements, explaining how that result changes what the pruning method appears to discover.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a nice example of the distinction between finding an interesting phenomenon and figuring out what actually explains it. With the lottery ticket hypothesis, you find that there are subnetworks that, with the right initialization, can train remarkably well. And that naturally raises the question: can we identify those subnetworks at initialization, without doing all the training first?

But then you have to be careful about what your experiments establish. If a method selects a sparse network at initialization and that network trains well, is it because it identified particularly important connections? Or did it just discover a good way to allocate sparsity across layers? One way to test that is to shuffle which connections survive within each layer while keeping the number of surviving connections fixed. If performance stays the same, that tells you something very different about what the method has accomplished.

That’s the scientific practice I find interesting: you propose an explanation, design a control that could undermine it, and then revise your explanation based on what happens. The method might still be useful. But understanding why it works is a separate question, and often that’s where the most interesting research begins.

r001.rationale: The response links pruning-at-initialization findings to measured training performance, explaining how comparing performance after shuffling surviving connections affects what researchers can conclude.
